steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Jiagu, a serverless system that improves resource utilization while staying efficient and practical. Explain how autoscaling and scheduling work in serverless platforms, why resources are wasted, why existing fixes face trade-offs, our two insights, the techniques built on them, and the headline evaluation results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Serverless computing, autoscaler and scheduler
2. Problem: low resource utilization and its two causes
3. Existing remedies (overcommitment, autoscaling) and their challenges
4. Two key insights: decoupling
5. Jiagu: pre-decision scheduling and dual-staged scaling
6. Prototype and evaluation results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- serverless: on-demand execution, autoscaling; zero to numerous instances per function in response to real-time demand
- autoscaler: predefined threshold per function = saturated value (e.g. RPS); creates instances when live load approaches it; prevents overload, guarantees QoS
- scheduler: places new instance on suitable node; checks resource requirements defined manually by developers

2. Problem
- traces from AliCloud and our public cloud (Huawei Cloud, top-five IaaS provider): most functions use small portion of allocated resources
- Figure 1, two factors: (①) users specify excessive resources for worst case, even saturated load can't use them; (②) load per instance fluctuates, under-loaded instances use fewer resources

3. Remedies and challenges
- ① overcommitment (scheduler deploys more instances per server); ② autoscaler keeps load near saturated load
- overcommitment risks performance degradation / QoS violation -> predict performance before scheduling
- prior predictor-based schedulers: progress but accuracy vs cost trade-off; interference on multiple resources from heterogeneous colocated functions
- e.g. specially designed ML models -> costly; cold start = scheduling + initialization latency, initialization optimized to < 1ms, inference (\sim 20ms or higher) new bottleneck
- public clouds still use heuristic policies -> limited improvement
- autoscaler must respond quickly, evict instances, free resources when load drops; faster = more cold starts -> utilization vs cold start trade-off

4. Insights
- decouple prediction and decision making: predict in advance for possible incoming instances, save results, fast path without model inference
- decouple resource releasing and instance eviction: send requests to fewer instances, cheaper, higher sensitivity

5. Jiagu techniques
- pre-decision scheduling: per deployed function, capacity on a server predicted in advance (max instances under current neighbors' interference without violating anyone's QoS); compare capacity with instance count
- asynchronous update keeps capacities up-to-date off critical path; concurrency-aware scheduling batches concurrent instances under load spikes
- >80% scheduling through fast path on real-world patterns
- dual-staged scaling: on load drop, re-route to fewer instances first (higher sensitivity); if load rises before eviction, re-route back with minimum overhead
- node full -> migrate idle instances to other nodes in advance, hide cold start overhead

6. Evaluation
- prototype on OpenFaaS; ServerlessBench, FunctionBench, real-world traces from Huawei Cloud
- vs state-of-the-art model-based scheduler: 81.0%–93.7% lower scheduling costs, 57.4%–69.3% lower cold start latency with cfork
- highest resource utilization among baselines, 54.8% higher instance density than Kubernetes

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Serverless computing makes managing cloud applications simpler with features such as on-demand execution and autoscaling. With autoscaling, cloud providers can dynamically deploy anywhere from zero to numerous instances to run a specific function depending on real-time demands, which optimizes performance and cost efficiency. Two main components are critical here: the autoscaler and the scheduler. The autoscaler uses a predefined threshold for each function, which is called the saturated value (e.g., requests per second, or RPS), and it triggers the creation of new instances when the live load gets close to this threshold. This way the autoscaler keeps instances from becoming overloaded and guarantees performance, which is usually measured as Quality-of-Service (QoS). When the autoscaler triggers creating a new instance, the scheduler has to schedule the instance to a suitable node. When it does this, the scheduler considers various things, including whether a node can meet the resource requirements of a function, which developers define manually.

But current serverless systems are still not efficient at using resources. Traces from AliCloud and from our public cloud (i.e., Huawei Cloud, a top-five IaaS provider) show that most serverless functions can only use a small part of the resources allocated to them. As shown in Figure 1, there are mainly two reasons for this. First, users usually consider the worst case to guarantee performance, so they give excessive resources to instances. Even when instances process a saturated load of requests, they cannot use the allocated resources. This causes the resource wastage of part ① in Figure 1. Second, in practice the user loads served by each instance fluctuate all the time. Instances that are under-loaded usually need fewer resources and are less able to use the resources, which causes the resource wastage of part ② in Figure 1.

To mitigate these two issues, serverless systems today can use overcommitment and autoscaling. First, for part ① in Figure 1, overcommitment is an intuitive solution, i.e., deploying more instances on a server. The scheduler could implement this, because the scheduler decides how instances are deployed. Second, for part ②, it could help to reduce the load fluctuations inside instances and try to keep the load of each instance close to the saturated load. The autoscaler can do this, since it is responsible for observing load fluctuations and changing the number of instances accordingly.

[Challenge 1: scheduling]
- overcommitment -> performance degradation, QoS violation -> predict performance before scheduling
- prior predictor-based schedulers: accuracy vs low cost trade-off (complex interference from heterogeneous colocated functions vs high overhead)
- specially designed ML models costly; cold start = scheduling + initialization; initialization < 1ms; inference (\sim 20ms or higher) new bottleneck
- public clouds use heuristic policies -> limited improvement

[Challenge 2: autoscaling]
- react quickly, evict, free resources; more sensitive scaling = more cold starts; trade-off

[Insights]
- decouple prediction and decision making -> fast path
- decouple resource releasing and instance eviction

[Jiagu]
- pre-decision scheduling, capacity, asynchronous update, concurrency-aware scheduling, >80% fast path
- dual-staged scaling, re-routing, migrating idle instances when node full

[Evaluation]
- OpenFaaS; ServerlessBench, FunctionBench, Huawei Cloud traces
- 81.0%–93.7% lower scheduling costs, 57.4%–69.3% lower cold start latency with cfork; 54.8% higher instance density than Kubernetes

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Serverless computing makes managing cloud applications simpler with features such as on-demand execution and autoscaling. With autoscaling, cloud providers can dynamically deploy anywhere from zero to numerous instances to run a specific function depending on real-time demands, which optimizes performance and cost efficiency. Two main components are critical here: the autoscaler and the scheduler. The autoscaler uses a predefined threshold for each function, which is called the saturated value (e.g., requests per second, or RPS), and it triggers the creation of new instances when the live load gets close to this threshold. This way the autoscaler keeps instances from becoming overloaded and guarantees performance, which is usually measured as Quality-of-Service (QoS). When the autoscaler triggers creating a new instance, the scheduler has to schedule the instance to a suitable node. When it does this, the scheduler considers various things, including whether a node can meet the resource requirements of a function, which developers define manually.

But current serverless systems are still not efficient at using resources. Traces from AliCloud and from our public cloud (i.e., Huawei Cloud, a top-five IaaS provider) show that most serverless functions can only use a small part of the resources allocated to them. As shown in Figure 1, there are mainly two reasons for this. First, users usually consider the worst case to guarantee performance, so they give excessive resources to instances. Even when instances process a saturated load of requests, they cannot use the allocated resources. This causes the resource wastage of part ① in Figure 1. Second, in practice the user loads served by each instance fluctuate all the time. Instances that are under-loaded usually need fewer resources and are less able to use the resources, which causes the resource wastage of part ② in Figure 1.

To mitigate these two issues, serverless systems today can use overcommitment and autoscaling. First, for part ① in Figure 1, overcommitment is an intuitive solution, i.e., deploying more instances on a server. The scheduler could implement this, because the scheduler decides how instances are deployed. Second, for part ②, it could help to reduce the load fluctuations inside instances and try to keep the load of each instance close to the saturated load. The autoscaler can do this, since it is responsible for observing load fluctuations and changing the number of instances accordingly.

However, it is hard to apply the two approaches effectively at a practical cost. First, overcommitment can lead to performance degradation and QoS violation, so it is common practice to predict performance before scheduling an instance to avoid violating QoS. But it is hard to predict the performance of instances accurately at a practical cost. Prior predictor-based schedulers have made a lot of progress, but they do not achieve both high accuracy and low cost, because the two goals can be a trade-off: to predict accurately you need to consider complex interference on multiple resources from highly heterogeneous colocated functions, but the complex computation unavoidably brings high overheads. For example, some prior works predict with specially designed machine learning models, which is costly for scheduling. Cold start latency mainly consists of scheduling latency and instance initialization latency, and a lot of work has optimized initialization to even < 1ms, so scheduling with inference (\sim 20ms or higher) could become a new bottleneck. As a compromise, public clouds today still use heuristic policies for scheduling, so they fail to predict performance accurately and only give limited improvement in resource utilization.

Second, to use resources efficiently when the load fluctuates, the autoscaler has to respond quickly to the load variation, evict instances and free the resources when the load drops. Intuitively, the faster autoscaling reacts to load fluctuations, the more efficiently resources can be used. But more sensitive and frequent scaling also means more additional cold starts, so there is a trade-off between resource utilization and cold start overheads. Achieving both goals at the same time is hard.

We have two key insights to tackle these challenges. First, the trade-off between scheduling costs and efficiency happens because these complex decisions have to be made at scheduling time, which involves costly predictions. So it can help to decouple prediction and decision making. Specifically, we can predict the performance of possible incoming instances in advance and save the results. If the incoming instance matches the scenario predicted in advance, scheduling can be done by just checking the prepared decisions, without model inference. This gives a fast path for scheduling.

Second, the trade-off between resource utilization and cold starts comes from the fact that instances do not release resources until they are evicted. Instead, we can decouple releasing resources and evicting instances. Specifically, operations like sending requests to fewer instances can have a similar effect of releasing resources as eviction. Releasing resources without evicting instances can be less costly, so it can be applied with higher sensitivity to get better resource utilization.

Based on these two insights, we propose Jiagu, a serverless system that harmonizes efficiency and practicability in improving resource utilization, and it tackles the challenges with two techniques. First, Jiagu does accurate and low cost performance prediction with pre-decision scheduling, which decouples prediction and decision making and gives a scheduling fast path without inference. For every function deployed on a server, Jiagu uses a model to predict in advance their capacities on that server. The capacity of a function is the maximum number of its instances that can be deployed on the server under the interference of the current neighbors without violating anyone's QoS. To schedule a new instance of a deployed function, Jiagu just compares the capacity of the function with the number of its instances to decide whether the scheduling can succeed. Jiagu also has an asynchronous update approach, which keeps the capacities up-to-date without putting model inference on the scheduling critical path, and it uses concurrency-aware scheduling to batch the scheduling of concurrent incoming instances when load spikes happen. Results with real-world patterns show that >80% of scheduling goes through the fast path.

Second, Jiagu has a dual-staged scaling method. When the load drops, before instances are evicted, Jiagu first adjusts the routing with a higher sensitivity and sends requests to fewer instances, which releases some of the resources of the instances. Then, if the load rises again before the idle instances are evicted, Jiagu can make the instances work again by re-routing with minimum overhead. Third, for the case where a node is full and the idle instances on it cannot be converted to the saturated state, Jiagu migrates idle instances to other nodes in advance to hide the overhead of the cold starts that are needed.

We built a prototype of Jiagu on an open-source serverless system, OpenFaaS. We evaluate it with ServerlessBench, FunctionBench, and applications with real-world traces from Huawei Cloud. The results show that on real-world traces, compared to a state-of-the-art model-based serverless scheduler, Jiagu has 81.0%–93.7% lower scheduling costs and 57.4%–69.3% lower cold start latency with cfork. It also gets the highest resource utilization compared to all baseline schedulers (54.8% higher instance density than Kubernetes).

steps.text:
Serverless computing [1] simplifies the management of cloud applications with features like on-demand execution and autoscaling. Through autoscaling, cloud providers can dynamically deploy zero to numerous instances to run a specific function in response to real-time demands, optimizing performance and cost efficiency. Two main components are critical to this process: the autoscaler and the scheduler. The autoscaler uses a predefined threshold for each function, called the saturated value (e.g., requests per second, or RPS), and triggers the creation of new instances as needed when the live load approaches this threshold [2,3]. In this way, the autoscaler prevents instances from becoming overloaded and guarantees performance, which is generally measured in terms of Quality-of-Service (QoS). When the autoscaler triggers the creation of a new instance, the scheduler is responsible for scheduling the instance to a suitable node. In doing so, the scheduler accounts for various aspects, including whether a node can meet a function's resource requirements, which developers define manually.

However, current serverless systems still fall short in utilizing resources efficiently. According to traces from AliCloud [4] and our public cloud (i.e., Huawei Cloud, a top-five IaaS provider [5]), most serverless functions can only utilize a small portion of their allocated resources. As illustrated in Figure 1, the issue mainly results from two factors. First, to guarantee performance, users usually consider the worst case and thus specify excessive resources for instances. Even when instances are processing a saturated load of requests, they cannot utilize the allocated resources, which causes the resource wastage of part ① in Figure 1. Second, in practice, the user loads served by each instance fluctuate continuously. Under-loaded instances usually require fewer resources and are less able to utilize them, resulting in the resource wastage of part ② in Figure 1.

To mitigate the two issues, serverless systems today can leverage overcommitment [4,6] and autoscaling [7]. First, for part ① in Figure 1, overcommitment is an intuitive solution, i.e., deploying more instances on a server. This could be implemented by the scheduler, as the scheduler is responsible for deciding how instances are deployed. Second, for part ②, it could help to reduce the load fluctuations within instances, trying to keep each instance's load close to the saturated load. This can be achieved by the autoscaler, which is responsible for observing load fluctuations and adjusting the number of instances accordingly.

Nevertheless, it is challenging to apply the two approaches effectively at a practical cost. First, since overcommitment may lead to performance degradation and QoS violation, it is common practice to predict performance before scheduling an instance. However, it is challenging to predict instances' performance accurately at a practical cost. Although prior predictor-based schedulers have made great progress [4,8,9,10,11,12,13], they fall short of achieving both high accuracy and low cost, since the two goals can be a trade-off: accurate prediction requires considering complex interference on multiple resources imposed by highly heterogeneous colocated functions, but the complex computation inevitably introduces high overheads. For example, some prior works predict with specially designed machine learning models [8], which is costly for scheduling. Since cold start latency mainly consists of scheduling latency and instance initialization latency, and initialization has been optimized by a lot of work to even < 1ms, scheduling with inference (\sim 20ms or higher) could become a new bottleneck [14]. As a compromise, public clouds today still use heuristic policies for scheduling, thus failing to predict performance accurately and providing limited improvement in resource utilization.

Second, to utilize resources efficiently under load fluctuation, the autoscaler needs to respond quickly to load variation, evicting instances and freeing resources when the load drops. Intuitively, the faster autoscaling reacts to load fluctuations, the more efficiently resources can be used. However, more sensitive and frequent scaling also means more additional cold starts, resulting in a trade-off between resource utilization and cold start overheads. Achieving both goals simultaneously is challenging.

We present two key insights to tackle these challenges. First, the trade-off between scheduling costs and efficiency arises because these complex decisions must be made at scheduling time, which involves costly predictions. Therefore, it can be beneficial to decouple prediction and decision making. Specifically, we can predict the performance of possible incoming instances in advance and save the results. If an incoming instance matches the scenario predicted in advance, scheduling can be done by directly checking the prepared decisions without model inference, providing a scheduling fast path.

Second, the trade-off between resource utilization and cold starts arises because instances do not release resources until they are evicted. Instead, we can decouple resource releasing and instance eviction. Specifically, operations like sending requests to fewer instances can have a similar effect of releasing resources as eviction. Releasing resources without evicting instances can be less costly, and can thus be applied with higher sensitivity for better resource utilization.

Inspired by these two insights, we propose Jiagu, a serverless system that harmonizes efficiency and practicability in improving resource utilization, tackling the challenges with two techniques. First, Jiagu achieves accurate and low cost performance prediction with pre-decision scheduling, which decouples prediction and decision making and provides a scheduling fast path without inference. For every function deployed on a server, Jiagu uses a model to predict their capacities on that server in advance. A function's capacity is the maximum number of its instances that can be deployed on the server under the interference of current neighbors without violating anyone's QoS. To schedule a new instance of a deployed function, Jiagu only needs to compare the function's capacity with the number of its instances to determine whether the scheduling can succeed. Moreover, Jiagu uses an asynchronous update approach, which keeps the capacities up-to-date without adding model inference to the scheduling critical path, and applies concurrency-aware scheduling to batch the scheduling of concurrent incoming instances when load spikes occur. Results with real-world patterns show that >80% of scheduling goes through the fast path.

Second, Jiagu uses a dual-staged scaling method. When the load drops, before instances are evicted, Jiagu first adjusts the routing with higher sensitivity, sending requests to fewer instances and thus releasing some of the instances' resources. Then, if the load rises again before the idle instances are evicted, Jiagu can put the instances back to work by re-routing with minimum overhead. Third, to cope with the case where a node is full and the idle instances on it cannot be converted to the saturated state, Jiagu migrates idle instances to other nodes in advance to hide the overhead of the required cold starts.

We present a prototype of Jiagu based on an open-source serverless system, OpenFaaS [15]. We evaluate it using ServerlessBench [16], FunctionBench [17], and applications with real-world traces from Huawei Cloud. The results show that on real-world traces, compared to a state-of-the-art model-based serverless scheduler [8], Jiagu incurs 81.0%–93.7% lower scheduling costs and 57.4%–69.3% lower cold start latency with cfork [18]. It also achieves the highest resource utilization among all baseline schedulers (54.8% higher instance density than Kubernetes).
